courses.title: Flow Cytometry Fundamentals
courses.description: Your samples just arrived. We'll set up the experiment, draw the first gate, and solve a spillover mystery to see why and how the data is compensated.

steps.text:
Welcome to Karcytics Flow Cytometry! 🧬

Imagine, you are a busy graduate student, and you isolated cells from three different mouse tissues: spleen, thymus and bone marrow. However, much to your dismay, you forgot to label the samples with the type of tissue they came from! Today's mystery: 3 unknown samples — one is Spleen, one is Thymus, one is Bone Marrow. Immune cells distributions look different from organ to organ, and by the end of Course 3 you'll have a confident, evidence-based answer for which is which. (Course 4 goes even deeper if you want it — but it's not required to crack the case.)

Let's start by loading our files.

Make a prediction 🔮

The thymus is where T cells mature and undergo positive and negative selection. Which cells do you expect the thymus sample to have *very few* of? There's no wrong answer — Course 3 will tell you.

choices.text: B cells
T cells
Immune cells of any kind

steps.text:
What you'll walk away with 🎯

By the end of this course, you'll be able to:
• Import raw FCS files and correctly tag every tube's role
• Explain why compensation is necessary, and apply a spillover matrix
• Draw your first gate, **Cells**, from scatter alone
• Read a spillover matrix and judge whether it is doing its job

These are the exact skills you'd use on a real cytometer.

Do you need to download the tutorial dataset files?

If you haven't downloaded them yet, I can fetch them for you now (~100MB). If you already have them, you can skip this step.
Preparing your tutorial files...

Getting your 10 tutorial files ready 📂

If they're already on this computer, this is instant. Otherwise Karcytics is downloading them now from the tutorial dataset (~100MB) — this only happens once, and may take a minute on a slower connection.
steps.failure_hint: Still downloading the tutorial files — this can take about a minute on a slower connection.

steps.text: Locating your files...
Let's get your files in. Click **➕ Add Samples** (highlighted) to open the file picker — your 10 tutorial files are waiting in Downloads → **Karcytics CytoAcademy Flow Files**. Select all 10.

variants.text: Let's get your files in. Click **➕ Add Samples** (highlighted) to open the file picker — {…}. Select all 10.

steps.text: Scanning files — checking all 10 samples loaded correctly…
Checking what went wrong...

Oops — you've loaded an incorrect sample that doesn't belong in this tutorial.

I've automatically removed it for you! Let's continue.

Hmm — I couldn't find all 10 samples.

Make sure you selected the Blank, PI, all 5 FMOs, and Samples A, B, C from the picker. Please load the rest!

One concept before we go further: Groups 📁

Look at the **Groups** panel in the sidebar — every sample you just imported sits under one default group, **All Samples**. A Group is simply a named subset of your samples, and it controls something important: gating actions (and later, locked axis scales) only propagate to OTHER samples in the SAME group.

Since all 10 of your samples are currently in **All Samples**, a gate you draw on one sample will automatically apply to the rest — that's the propagation you'll rely on throughout this course.

Why make a custom group? If you're analyzing completely different tissue types that need different gating strategies, or juggling multiple experiments in the same workspace, separating them into different groups ensures their gates don't interfere. You won't need to do that for this tutorial, though.

All 10 files are in! ✅

Let's assign the purpose of each file — we call this a **Role**. The roles are:
• **Blank** → Unstained (no dye — background autofluorescence)
• **PI** → Single Stain (one dye to correct spectral overlap)
• **FMO_*** → FMO Control (all dyes minus one — identifies true background for gating)
• **Samples A/B/C** → Full Panel (experiment samples)

We'll assign them one step at a time.

Quick check ✅

Cells were labeled with an APC-conjugated anti-CD45 antibody. Later you'll need to know how bright a cell can be *without* CD45. Which file shows you that?
steps.explanation: The APC FMO includes all fluorophores except APC, matching the spillover into the APC channel while lacking true CD45 signal. Its APC signal is background, defining the CD45-negative boundary.

choices.text: Blank
choices.feedback: Close, but the blank contains no fluorophores, so it does not capture the spillover from the other dyes into the APC detector. Its lower boundary is therefore too low.

choices.text: FMO APC
Sample A
choices.feedback: Sample A contains APC-conjugated anti-CD45, its true APC signal prevents assessment of the spillover/background into the APC channel

steps.text: Checking the Properties Panel...

One thing first: the **Properties Panel** (right) is showing its **Histogram** view, and we need the sample details instead.

Click **Properties** at the top of the panel (highlighted) to switch back.
steps.failure_hint: Click **Properties** at the top of the Properties Panel on the right.

steps.text:
**Step 1 of 4** — Blank sample.

In the **Sample List** (left, highlighted), double click on **Blank**. Then in the **Properties Panel** (right, highlighted), find the Role dropdown and set it to **Unstained**.

I'll advance automatically once it's set!
steps.failure_hint: Double-check you selected **Blank** in the Sample List, then set its Role to **Unstained** in the Properties Panel.

steps.text:
**Step 2 of 4** — PI file.

**PI (Propidium Iodide)** is our viability dye — just one dye, which makes it the perfect single-stain control for its channel.

Double click on the PI file in the **Sample List** and set its Role to **Single Stain**. Karcytics will detect it automatically.
steps.failure_hint: Double-check you selected the **PI** file in the Sample List, then set its Role to **Single Stain**.

steps.text:
**Step 3 of 4** — FMO controls.

**FMO (Fluorescence Minus One)**. Each FMO file has every fluorophore *except* one, letting us clearly see the boundary between the true negative background and actual positive signals for that missing dye.

Doing this one-by-one is tedious! Click **🏷️ Bulk Assign Roles** (highlighted in the ribbon).

In the dialog, select all 5 FMO files, set them to the **FMO Control** role, and click Assign.
steps.failure_hint: Make sure you selected all 5 FMO files in **Bulk Assign Roles** and set them to **FMO Control**.

steps.text:
**Step 4 of 4** — mystery samples.

Use the **🏷️ Bulk Assign Roles** button again to select Samples A, B, and C and set their Role to **Full Panel**.

I'll keep an eye on your progress and we'll move forward once all the tubes are set up.
steps.failure_hint: Make sure Samples A, B, and C are all set to **Full Panel** via Bulk Assign Roles.

steps.text:
Phase 1 in three lines 📝

• **Import:** your 10 files are in, all in one group.
• **Roles** tell Karcytics what each tube is for: Single Stains help measure spillover, Full Panels are the samples you analyse, and FMOs show where 'negative' ends for gating.
• FMOs are left out of the final statistics, so they don't skew your sample averages.

Phase 2 — Your first gate 🎯

Gating means drawing regions on plots to select specific cell populations — and we do it hierarchically: each new gate narrows down INSIDE the last one, like a funnel, so everything downstream is automatically purified of whatever you excluded earlier.

The hierarchy we're heading for:
**All Events → Cells → Live → Leukocytes**

Today we draw **Cells**. It uses scatter only, no dyes, so it can come before compensation. First, switch to the **Gating** tab.
Click the **Gating** tab (highlighted) at the top. This shows the polygon, rectangle, and range drawing tools.

Before drawing any gates, we start with the **Blank** (Unstained) sample.

In the **Sample List**, find the **Blank** file and double-click it. This opens its scatter plot in the centre canvas.

We use the unstained sample first because it has no dyes, making it the perfect baseline to find the physical cell population based purely on size and complexity.
Checking opened sample...

Oops! You opened the wrong sample.

Please double-click the **Blank** sample to open it.

Read the plot 💡

**FSC** (forward scatter) tracks a particle's size; **SSC** (side scatter) tracks how much is inside it. Debris is fragments: small and simple. Where on this plot does it sit?
steps.explanation: Fragments produce little forward scatter and have little internal structure to scatter light sideways. Because forward and side scatter can distinguish intact cells from debris without any fluorescent label, this FSC/SSC gate is typically the first step.

choices.text: Bottom-left: low FSC, low SSC
Top-right: high FSC, high SSC
choices.feedback: That's big, granular cells. Fragments scatter little light either way.

choices.text: Bottom-right: high FSC, low SSC
choices.feedback: High FSC means large. Fragments are small.

steps.text:
Now look past the debris 🔍

Above and to the right of the dense lower-left cloud there's a second, looser cluster: higher **FSC** *and* higher **SSC**.

Remember, this tube is unstained, so this is pure light scatter. What does that position tell you about those cells?
steps.explanation: Higher FSC means a bigger cell; higher SSC means more inside it (granules, organelles, a lobed nucleus). Small, smooth lymphocytes sit low on both axes; granular myeloid cells like granulocytes sit up and right. So even without antibodies, scatter hints at which cell types a tissue holds.

choices.text: They're larger and more internally complex (more granules and organelles)
They carry more fluorescent dye
choices.feedback: This sample has no dye at all. FSC and SSC are scattered laser light, so they describe the cell's physical build.

choices.text: They're dead or dying cells
choices.feedback: Dying cells usually shrink, so FSC drops. Scatter alone can't confirm death, which is why we add the viability dye (PI) later.

choices.text: It just means there are more of them
choices.feedback: A position on the plot is a measurement per cell. How many cells there are shows up as how dense the cloud is.

steps.text:
**Gate 1: Cells**

The current plot shows **FSC-A** (cell size) vs **SSC-A** (cell complexity). You'll see:
• 2 main clusters of cells
• The debris cloud in the bottom-left corner
• A good chunk of splatter throughout the entire canvas

We want to draw a gate that excludes the debris. This ensures all downstream analysis excludes junk events.

When you draw the gate in the next step, a popup will ask you for its name. Be sure to call it **Cells**!

Before you draw, let's open a second view of the gate.

At the top of the **Properties Panel** (right), click **Histogram** (highlighted).

It shows the same cells as two histograms — **FSC-A** on top, **SSC-A** below — and updates live while you draw.
steps.failure_hint: Click **Histogram** at the top of the Properties Panel on the right.

steps.text:
Draw the gate:

1. Click **Polygon** in the Gating ribbon (highlighted above)
2. Click each vertex around the oval cell cloud on the plot (highlighted)
3. Double-click to close the polygon
4. Type **Cells** in the popup and hit Enter!

As you click, watch the **histograms** on the right (highlighted): the coloured part is what your gate keeps, the grey is what it leaves out.

Your gate will be evaluated automatically once you finish drawing.
steps.stuck_hint_text: Still there? Click **Polygon** in the Gating ribbon, then click around the cell cloud and double-click to close the shape.

steps.text: Evaluating your gate...
I renamed the gate to **Cells** for you. Let's proceed!

That gate didn't quite match the shape!

I deleted it for you. Make sure you cover the main cluster of cells while excluding the debris at the bottom left.

Try drawing it again.

Gate drawn. ✅

The **Histogram** view is there whenever you want a second look at a gate. The steps ahead read the gate's statistics, so click **Properties** (highlighted) to switch the panel back.
steps.failure_hint: Click **Properties** at the top of the Properties Panel on the right.

steps.text:
Perfect shape! 🎯

Notice that your new gate has appeared in the **Gating Hierarchy** panel on the left.

This hierarchy tracks all populations. By default, the gates you apply to one sample will propagate to all other samples in the same group.

Made a mistake while gating? **Ctrl+Z** (**Cmd+Z** on a Mac) undoes your last change.

Great job! 🎯

Typically, the next step is gating for **Singlets** to remove clumps of cells (doublets). You'd do this by plotting **FSC-A** vs FSC-H and drawing a narrow diagonal gate down the center line.

Doublets have a disproportionately larger Area than Height, so they appear as a separate population shifted to the right of the diagonal. You would filter them out by only keeping the events on the diagonal.

Our dataset doesn't include the -H or -W parameters, so we won't gate for singlets today, but it's a crucial step in real experiments!

Phase 2 in three lines 📝

• **Gates** are regions you draw around cells; each one narrows down inside the last, like a funnel.
• **FSC** (size) and **SSC** (inner complexity) need no dye, so the **Cells** gate can come first.
• Gates spread to every sample in the same **group**, and **Ctrl+Z / Cmd+Z** undoes a mistake.

Phase 3 — Compensation ⚖️

Every gate after **Cells** uses the light from the dyes. Before you trust it, there's a puzzle to solve. Click the **Compensation** tab (highlighted) at the top.

This switch (highlighted) turns **compensation** on or off for every sample. It's **ON** now: that's what the ✦ next to each sample means.

Click it to turn compensation **OFF**, so you see the readings exactly as the cytometer recorded them.
steps.failure_hint: Click **Compensation: ON ✦** in the Compensation tab's header.

steps.text: Compensation is **OFF** (the ✦ marks are gone). Go back to the **Gating** tab and double-click **Sample A** in the **Sample List**.
steps.failure_hint: Open the **Gating** tab, then double-click **Sample A** in the Sample List.

steps.text:
Put two dyes on the plot:
• **X:** → **PE-A** (the CD4 marker, on T helper cells)
• **Y:** → **PerCP-Cy5-5-A** (where **PI** is read; PI marks dead cells)
steps.failure_hint: Set the **X:** dropdown to **PE-A** and the **Y:** dropdown to **PerCP-Cy5-5-A**.

steps.text:
The mystery 🕵️

Look at the brightest CD4 cells (far right). They sit higher on the PI axis than the dim ones, and many look PI-positive. PI marks dead cells. Are bright CD4 T cells especially likely to be dead?

choices.text: Yes, many of them are dead
Something else makes them look PI-positive
Can't tell from this plot

steps.text: To solve it, look at the light itself. Click the **Spectral** tab (highlighted) at the top.

The **Spectral Viewer** 🌈

Karcytics read your panel's 6 fluorescence channels from the files and plotted each **dye's** real, measured spectrum from **FPbase**, an open database of dyes (cited under the viewer): FITC, PE, PI, Pacific Blue, APC-Cy7 and APC.

Each legend entry shows the **marker** the dye is attached to, like **CD45 (APC-A)**. CD45 is a protein on the cell with no colour of its own; the colour comes from the dye on the antibody. So spillover is about dyes, not markers.

PI is the odd one out: it isn't an antibody tag but a dye in its own right, read in the **PerCP-Cy5.5** detector, so Karcytics plotted PI's own spectrum.

Where does spillover come from? ⛰️

A dye doesn't glow at one exact colour. It glows across a broad hill of wavelengths, often 100 nm wide or more. Each detector sits under the peak of one dye's hill, but the hills' shoulders reach into neighbouring detectors.

Find **CD4 (PE)** and **PI** in the legend. PE's hill runs on past 600 nm, right into the colours where PI is read.

Spillover in action 🌈

Some of PE's light lands in the detector where PI is read. Without compensation, how does a cell that's bright for PE (CD4) but has no PI look?
steps.explanation: That's a strong lead for your 'dead' CD4 cells. But plenty of curves overlap here, and not every overlap causes trouble. The next idea, lasers, explains which ones do.

choices.text: PI-negative, as it should
choices.feedback: The PI detector still catches PE's shoulder, so its reading climbs even though there's no PI.

choices.text: Dimmer for PE
choices.feedback: Spillover adds to the neighbouring detector; it doesn't take away from PE's own reading.

choices.text: Falsely PI-positive, so it looks dead

steps.text:
Lasers light the dyes 🔦

A dye only glows when light of the right colour hits it:
• **EX** (excitation): the colours that make the dye glow. It tells you which laser lights it, e.g. the 488 nm blue laser.
• **AB** (absorbance): the colours it soaks up, close to EX.
• **EM** (emission): the colours it glows back, caught by a detector.

Your cytometer has three lasers: violet (405 nm), blue (488 nm) and red (640 nm), and each detector sits behind one of them. Try the **AB / EX / EM** buttons (highlighted) to see each set of curves.
Switching the emission curves back on...

Do lasers matter? 🔦

Pacific Blue's emission overlaps FITC's. But Pacific Blue is lit by the violet laser, and FITC's detector sits behind the blue laser, which barely excites Pacific Blue. How much Pacific Blue light ends up in FITC's detector?
steps.explanation: Spillover needs both: a dye's light must overlap the detector's colours, and that detector's laser must light the dye. PE and PI are both lit by the blue laser, so their overlap really counts.

choices.text: A lot: their curves overlap
choices.feedback: Overlapping emission only counts if the dye is glowing in that detector's laser beam. The blue laser leaves Pacific Blue nearly dark.

choices.text: Very little: the blue laser barely lights it
Exactly the overlap shown on the plot
choices.feedback: The plot shows emission only. Whether that light is produced in the right beam depends on the laser too.

steps.text:
Reading the overlap callouts 🔍

Karcytics marks every pair of emission curves that overlap: the hatched white area is the shared light, and each callout gives an **Overlap integral %**. Click a callout to dismiss it.

Those % come from emission curves alone. Lasers and filters change the real spillover, which is why labs measure it with controls.

Overlap isn't automatically a problem 🧠

Two overlaps in your panel: **CD3** (Pacific Blue) with **B220** (FITC), and **CD4** (PE) with **PI**, the live/dead dye read in the PerCP-Cy5.5 detector. Left uncorrected, which one could quietly distort your results?
steps.explanation: Spillover between PE and PI makes bright, live CD4 cells look dead, so a live/dead gate would throw real CD4 T cells away. Overlap matters when both signals can sit on one cell, or one drives a gating decision.

choices.text: CD3 with B220
choices.feedback: T cells and B cells are separate lineages, so spilled light can't invent a believable double-positive. And different lasers (405 vs 488 nm) light the two dyes, so little of that light reaches the other's detector.

choices.text: CD4 with PI
Neither: they're well under 50%
choices.feedback: A few percent of a very bright dye is enough to push a negative cell past a gate. The size of the overlap matters less than what the two signals mean.

steps.text: Now put the theory to work: click the **Learning Compensation** sub-tab (highlighted) just above the plot.

The **Learning Compensation** deck 📚

Seven short slides that take you from overlapping light to a full matrix, with numbers from your own dyes. On each one:
• **👉 Your turn** (top left) says what to do
• **💡 Show me** (top right) draws it if you're stuck
• **🧮** does any sum for you

Press **Got it** and I'll stay out of the way until you finish the last slide.
steps.stuck_hint_text: Still going? 💡 Show me on any slide draws what it needs.

steps.text: Deck done! 🎓 Time to solve the mystery. Open the **Compensation** tab and click the switch to turn compensation back **ON**. Every sample gets the spillover taken off, as you did on the slider.
steps.failure_hint: In the **Compensation** tab, click **Compensation: OFF** in the header.

steps.text: Compensation is **ON** again (the ✦ marks are back). Go to the **Gating** tab (highlighted): Sample A is still on PE vs PI.

Mystery solved 🔍

Far fewer of the bright CD4 cells look PI-positive now. Most of that 'PI' was **PE light landing in the PI detector**: spillover. The cells weren't dead; the reading was wrong.

You predicted: *{answer:c1_dead_or_not}*.

Without compensation, a live/dead gate here would have thrown away healthy CD4 T cells.

Where did that correction come from? 🗂

The cytometer measured the spillover itself, with single-stain tubes like the ones on the deck's last slide, and saved it in your files (a **$SPILL** keyword). Karcytics applied it on loading: the ✦ on every sample.

Click the **Compensation** tab (highlighted) to see those numbers.

Click **📄 Extract from FCS** (highlighted).

This reads the matrix from the file and opens it on the **Matrix** page.

Reading the matrix, part 1: rows 👉

Each **row** is a **dye**. This one is **PE**'s row: it says where PE's light goes. The 1 is PE in its own detector; the other numbers are how much of it spills into each other detector.

Part 2: columns 👇

Each **column** is a **detector**. This one is the **PerCP-Cy5.5** detector, where PI is read: it says how much of every dye's light lands there.

Read the matrix 🔢

This cell (highlighted) is where PE's row meets the PI detector's column: the spillover behind your mystery. How much of **PE**'s signal lands in the **PerCP-Cy5-5** detector?
steps.explanation: 0.30 means 30%: for every 100 units of PE, the PI detector reads 30 extra. It's the largest value in this matrix, which is why bright CD4 cells looked dead.

choices.feedback: That's the other direction: the PerCP-Cy5-5 row, PE column. Start from the PE row.
That's the diagonal: a dye in its own detector, always 1. Look along the PE row.

steps.text:
The switch flips every sample at once. To *judge* a matrix, the preview shows before and after side by side.

1. Click the **0.3000** cell (PE row, PerCP-Cy5-5 column). The preview switches to that pair: the dye on X, the detector on Y.
2. Set **Sample** to **Sample A**.
steps.failure_hint: Click the 0.3000 cell in the PE-A row, then choose Sample A in the **Sample** dropdown above the plots.

steps.text:
Before and after 👀

Left: the raw signal. Right: the same cells with this matrix. The big cloud is PE-bright cells that carry no PI. With a good matrix, how should it sit on the **After** plot?
steps.explanation: Level is the goal, exactly as on the deck's slider: being bright for PE should say nothing about the PI detector. Tilted up means the value is too low; pushed down means too high.

choices.text: Climbing diagonally as PE gets brighter
choices.feedback: That's the raw plot: the brighter the PE, the more of it spills into the other detector.

choices.text: Dipping below the PE-negative cells
choices.feedback: That's over-compensation, like pushing the deck's slider too far: more is taken off than spilled in.

choices.text: Level with the PE-negative cells

steps.text: One tube is one opinion. Set **Sample** (highlighted) to **All samples**: one row of plots per tube, drawn in the background.
steps.failure_hint: Open the **Sample** dropdown and pick All samples, at the bottom of the list.

steps.text:
Scroll through the rows 🧪

One matrix is applied to every tube. Why check it on all of them rather than on one?
steps.explanation: A tube with few bright cells for a dye can't show whether that dye's value is right. Tubes that are bright there can. Looking across all of them covers every dye.

choices.text: A value can look right on one tube and be off on another
Each tube needs its own matrix
choices.feedback: One matrix serves the experiment: same dyes, same cytometer settings. The check is that it holds everywhere.

choices.text: Only full-panel samples get compensated
choices.feedback: Controls are compensated too: an FMO only sets a threshold if it was treated like the samples.

steps.text:
Compensation in three lines 📝

• **Why:** a dye's light also lands in other dyes' detectors (spillover), and can fake a signal, like 'dead' CD4 cells.
• **What the number means:** 0.30 = for every 100 units of PE, the PI detector reads 30 extra. Compensation takes that much off every cell.
• **How to check it:** single-dye cells should sit level with the negative cells, not climbing and not dipping, in every tube.

One for next time 🔮

In Course 2 you'll estimate a matrix from your **FMO** tubes. Each FMO lacks one dye, and shows what spills into that dye's detector. There is no PerCP-Cy5-5 FMO. What will the estimate say about spill into PerCP-Cy5-5?

choices.text: Nothing: it has no tube to measure it from
About the same 0.30 the file has
A rough value worked out from the other tubes

steps.text:
Saving your progress 💾

Course 2 builds on this workspace, so save it now (with compensation **ON**).

Click the **⚠️ Save Workspace** button (highlighted) at the top right.

Give it a name like **Learning flow with Cyto!** and click Save.
steps.failure_hint: Make sure compensation is **ON** (Compensation tab header), then click **⚠️ Save Workspace**, give it a name, and click Save.

All done! You've imported your samples, tagged their roles, drawn your first gate, and solved a spillover mystery. 🚀

Your workspace is saved. In Course 2, we will use this exact setup to gate out dead cells and find the Leukocytes.

Click Next to collect your badge!

steps.text:
Checking your workspace...

Making sure all 10 samples are loaded and compensated, roles are assigned, and the **Cells** gate exists — confirming the Course 1 workflow was opened correctly.
steps.failure_hint: This course picks up where Course 1 left off — make sure you opened the workspace you saved at the end of Course 1, with all samples, roles, compensation and the Cells gate in place.

steps.text:
Welcome to Course 2! 🎯

Your data is compensated and the **Cells** gate has removed the debris. Two more gates finish the clean-up, each drawn *inside* the one before:
**All Events → Cells → Live → Leukocytes**

Both sit on fluorescence channels, which is why compensation had to come first. So before the gates, one more look at the matrix: this time you'll build your own.

steps.section: Building a matrix from the FMO controls
steps.text:
Why build your own matrix? 🧮

In Course 1 you read the matrix the cytometer saved in the files. Two reasons to make one yourself:
• some files carry no matrix at all
• a second, independent estimate is the best check on the first

Your **FMO** tubes can provide one. You'll estimate it, compare it with the file's, and decide which to keep.

steps.section: Building a matrix from the FMO controls
steps.text: Click the **Compensation** tab (highlighted) at the top.

steps.section: Building a matrix from the FMO controls
steps.text: Set **Method** (highlighted) to **FMO controls**, and stay on the **⚙ Method setup** page.
steps.failure_hint: Open the **Method** dropdown and pick FMO controls; click **⚙ Method setup** if another page is showing.

steps.section: Building a matrix from the FMO controls
steps.text:
How the FMO method works 💡

An FMO tube has every dye but one. So whatever its *missing* dye's detector records must have leaked in from the others. Karcytics measures that leak in each FMO tube, then solves all of them together for the matrix.

This is Karcytics' own method, not a published standard, so the page (highlighted) spells out every step and its limits. Read it once: a method you can't explain is one you can't defend.

steps.section: Building a matrix from the FMO controls
steps.text:
What it will use 🔎

The table shows each FMO tube, the dye it **Lacks**, and **How we know**. The *e450* tube's name doesn't say Pacific Blue. How was it placed?
steps.explanation: A tube without a dye is the odd one out in that dye's detector. That is worked out once and kept; the Missing dye dropdown lets you correct it.

choices.text: It is dim in that channel, unlike the other FMO tubes
From the tube's name
choices.feedback: Names are only a fallback guess. The How we know column says this one came from its data.

choices.text: From its Role
choices.feedback: The role only says it is an FMO control, not which dye was left out.

steps.section: Building a matrix from the FMO controls
steps.text:
The blind spot 🕳️

Look at the table's last row: **(no FMO control) · PerCP-Cy5-5-A · not estimated — left at 0**.

In Course 1 you predicted: *{answer:c1_fmo_blind_spot}*.

With no tube lacking that dye, the method has nothing to measure the leak from. It says so rather than guessing. Remember this detector: it is where PI is read.

steps.section: Building a matrix from the FMO controls
steps.text: Set **Fit on** (highlighted) to **Cells**, the gate you drew in Course 1.
steps.failure_hint: Open the **Fit on** dropdown near the top of Method setup and pick Cells.

steps.section: Building a matrix from the FMO controls
steps.text: The **Events used** column now counts only the events inside Cells. Why fit on those rather than on everything recorded?
steps.explanation: Fragments and aggregates glow for their own reasons. Let them into the fit and their signal is read as spill. This is why the Cells gate came before compensation.

Behind the Scenes: The **No-Jump** Rule

In Karcytics, the auto-zoom calculation only happens *once* the very first time you select a channel. From that point on, the view is completely locked for that channel across all samples in the group.

This guarantees that as you draw deeper gates and switch between controls and full samples, the plot won't aggressively jump around or zoom in. You will always maintain your bearings!

Welcome to Course 3! 🎯

Our **Leukocytes** are gated. Now let's identify who's actually inside that population: **T-cells** and **B-cells**, using two different gating techniques.

• Read the **Pipeline** view the way a real gating strategy gets documented

courses.title: Population Analysis: Run & Validate
courses.description: Let UMAP and HDBSCAN independently cluster Sample C with zero manual gates, then prove the result out against your own hand-gating.

steps.text:
Welcome to Course 4! 🧠

Course 3 left you with a hand-drawn hierarchy — Leukocytes, T-cells, B-cells, and the CD4/CD8 subsets — across all three samples.

This course hands that same data to an algorithm that has never seen your gates, and lets it draw its own conclusions.
Checking your gating tree from Course 3...

Missing a gate 🔍

Every sample needs **Leukocytes**, **T-cells**, and **B-cells** gated before Course 4 can continue — that's the foundation Course 3 built. Head back and finish that course first, then relaunch Course 4.
Your gating tree checks out! Click the 'Population Analysis' tab at the top.

Understanding UMAP 🧠

You have 6 fluorescence channels — every cell is a point in 6-dimensional space. **UMAP** (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is a dimension-reduction technique: it flattens that 6D cloud down onto a 2D map you can actually look at, the same way t-SNE does, while trying much harder to preserve both local neighborhoods and the broader shape between them.

Reading the map 🗺️

UMAP squeezes your marker channels onto just two axes. One cell lands at **x = 5**. What does that tell you about it?
steps.explanation: UMAP's axes measure nothing. What matters is which cells end up near each other: a tight island means those cells are similar across all the channels at once, often a real population you never gated.

choices.text: Its CD3 level is 5
choices.feedback: There's no CD3 axis. UMAP makes its axes up for the layout; they don't measure any marker.

choices.text: Nothing on its own; only its neighbors matter
It sits halfway between the dimmest and brightest cells
choices.feedback: The axes have no units and no direction of 'bright'. Only which cells land near it means anything.

steps.text:
When to trust it (and when not) ⚠️

UMAP is genuinely good at preserving *local* neighborhoods — which cells resemble which. Don't over-read the rest of the picture, though: the distance *between* islands, their relative size, and even the overall layout can shift with different parameters or a different random seed, even though the same real populations keep showing up. Treat 'these cells cluster together' as trustworthy; treat 'island A is twice as far from island B as island C' as decoration. That's exactly why this course has you cross-check the result against your own hand-gating later, instead of taking UMAP's word for it alone.

Want the deeper dive? 🎥

StatQuest's walkthrough is the clearest explanation of how UMAP actually works under the hood, if you want more than the summary I gave:

[Watch: UMAP, Main Ideas!!! (StatQuest)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m3s0Tgh8ofg)
In the sidebar, set **Sample** to 'Sample C'.

Why Sample C? 🧩

Course 3 confirmed Sample C is the **Spleen** — the one sample with mature T-cells *and* B-cells living side by side. That mix makes it the richest sample to hand to an unsupervised algorithm: there's more than one real population for it to actually have to separate.
Set **Population (Gate)** to 'Leukocytes'.

Why gate first? 🚫

You could run UMAP on **All Events**. Why give it **Leukocytes** instead?
steps.explanation: Debris and dead cells have no biological identity, but UMAP will still group them into islands. Gating to Leukocytes keeps them out, so every island is made of real, living cells, and the smaller input runs faster.

choices.text: Debris and dead cells would form fake islands
UMAP can't read scatter channels
choices.feedback: It can read any channel. The problem is what debris and dead cells would add, not which channels they're in.

choices.text: Fewer events, so the run is faster
It pushes the T-cell and B-cell islands further apart
choices.feedback: Distance between islands means little on a UMAP. Gating is about keeping junk events out of the map.

steps.text: In the channel list, **uncheck PI and CD45** — leave every other channel checked.

Why exclude these two? ✂️

**PI**'s job ended at the Live gate: the dead cells are already gone. Inside **Leukocytes**, why is **CD45** no use to UMAP either?
steps.explanation: You drew Leukocytes on CD45, so every cell left is CD45-positive. A channel that's high in every cell can't separate one population from another; it only adds noise for UMAP to wade through.

choices.text: It spills too much into the other channels
choices.feedback: Compensation already corrected spillover. The issue is what CD45 measures inside this gate.

choices.text: UMAP can't use the APC channel
choices.feedback: UMAP can use any channel. CD45 is left out for what it shows here, not where it's measured.

choices.text: Every cell here is CD45-positive, so it can't tell them apart

steps.section: Settings, grouped by the decision they make
steps.text:
Four settings shape the map 🗺️

**Neighbors**: how local UMAP's view is.
**Min Distance**: how tightly it packs similar cells (low for rare subtypes, high to see lineages).
**Distance Metric**: how it measures difference; Euclidean is the safe default.
**Random Seed**: makes the run repeatable. Change it to check a cluster isn't a one-off.

The defaults suit this run.

steps.section: Settings, grouped by the decision they make
steps.text:
Neighbors 🔗

This sets how many nearby cells UMAP looks at when deciding what 'close together' means. Say you're hunting a rare population of about 200 cells. Raise it or lower it?
steps.explanation: Low values (5–15) keep small, tight populations apart; high values (30–50) show how the major lineages relate. It's a judgment call about what you're looking for. The default, 15, is fine for this run.

choices.text: Lower, to keep fine local detail
Raise, so each cell sees more of its surroundings
choices.feedback: With many neighbors, a 200-cell group gets blended into the bigger populations around it.

choices.text: It makes no difference for rare cells
choices.feedback: It does: neighbors decides how local UMAP's view is, and a rare group needs a local view.

steps.section: Settings, grouped by the decision they make
steps.text:
UMAP slows down sharply on big data, so it works on a random share of the cells ⚡

Set **Events used** to 25%: plenty to represent every real population, and fast enough to try again.

steps.section: Settings, grouped by the decision they make
steps.text:
Check **Run HDBSCAN Auto-Clustering**.

Its **Min Cluster Size** (100) is the fewest cells it accepts as a cluster: smaller groups join a neighbour or become noise.

steps.section: Settings, grouped by the decision they make
steps.text:
A second opinion 🔬

UMAP already shows islands, so why run **HDBSCAN** too? It comes down to what it clusters. Which data does HDBSCAN group?
steps.explanation: HDBSCAN groups cells by density in the original marker data, with no human input. If its clusters line up with your hand-drawn gates, that's a measurement, not a plot that happened to look convincing.

choices.text: The 2-D picture UMAP draws
choices.feedback: Then it would only trace islands you can already see. It works on the marker data itself.

choices.text: The same marker data UMAP read, before flattening
The gates you drew in Course 3
choices.feedback: It never sees your gates. That's exactly why its agreement with them means something.

steps.text: Everything's configured. Click '🧬 Run Analysis' (highlighted).

This animation is real 🎬

What you're watching isn't decorative — it's built from Sample C's actual high-dimensional marker data, run through the real UMAP algorithm, while the full analysis keeps computing underneath it. Watch for 5 phases: your cells appearing in high-dimensional marker space, a fuzzy neighbor graph connecting similar cells, an initial rough 2D layout, that layout settling under force-directed motion, and finally the finished manifold — the same 'islands' you're about to explore.
Crunching the real numbers underneath that animation...

One thing before we dig into results 📜

That run just got saved to **History** (left sidebar). Every run you complete lands here, so if you tweak a parameter and run again later, your earlier runs aren't lost — pick any of them from this dropdown to instantly revisit its results, no recomputing needed. Picking **[ New Run ]** brings back the parameter panel so you can configure a fresh run.

The Plot Gallery 🖼️

Results are in! Each tile here is the same UMAP layout, colored by one marker's expression. Find the **CD3** tile — that's your T-cell island lighting up — then find **B220**, and watch a completely different island light up instead.

One more tile 🎯

If HDBSCAN found clusters, there's also an **Auto-Cluster ID** tile — every cell colored by which unsupervised cluster it landed in, with zero manual gates involved.

Why those two islands are different, biologically 🧬

CD3 and B220 didn't just happen to land in separate islands. **CD3** marks the T-cell receptor complex; **B220** is a B-cell-restricted isoform of CD45. T-cells and B-cells diverge early in development into consistently different signatures across the other channels too — so UMAP, which only ever looks at overall marker similarity and knows nothing about what any channel *means*, separates them anyway. That's the same T-cell/B-cell distinction you gated by hand in Course 3, arrived at here without drawing a single gate.
Click the 'Interactive Map' tab (highlighted).

Explore freely 🖱️

Move your cursor over any population on the map — a live panel will show you its local marker expression. Take a minute to hover around before continuing.

Keep in mind: this map reflects the **Leukocytes** gate and channel choices you made earlier. A different gating strategy upstream can lead to noticeably different clusters down here — this isn't the one true answer, it's *an* answer, shaped by the choices you made.

One more reminder ⚠️

The overall **shape** of this map, and where things sit on the x/y axes, carry no biological meaning by themselves — the axes aren't measuring anything. All that matters is which cells UMAP judged similar enough to sit close together.

Try a different lens 🔬

Use the dropdown above the map — it's currently showing **Auto-Cluster ID**. Switch it to the **FITC** marker (B220) and watch the B-cell population light up on the same map, no re-running required.

That's not decoration 🔬

That large lit-up island is real B220 signal — and B220 **was** one of the channels UMAP saw (only PI and CD45 were excluded). So this isn't an unseen-channel confirmation; it's proof the 2D layout UMAP built from *all* your marker channels together lines up with what gating on B220 alone would tell you — the unsupervised structure matches real biology, not an artifact of the projection.
Click the 'Population Statistics' tab (highlighted).

Cluster Statistics 📋

One row per cluster HDBSCAN found — its cell count and its % of the total. This is the same count you'd get by hand-gating, just produced without you drawing a single gate.

Marker Expression Heatmap 🌡️

One row per cluster, one column per marker — brighter red means higher expression. This is the **median** expression per marker per cluster, not the mean, which is exactly why it's the more outlier-robust number to trust for identifying which cluster is which population.

Expression Profiles 📊

The same heatmap numbers, redrawn as a 100%-stacked bar per cluster — easier to compare a cluster's whole marker *profile* at a glance than reading numbers cell by cell.

One cluster doesn't count 🚫

**Cluster ID -1** is HDBSCAN's noise bucket — cells it couldn't confidently assign to any real, dense population. It'll show up in every table here, but it's never a candidate for anything you export downstream.

Cross-checking the two methods 🔀

You now have two independent ways of finding B-cells: your hand-gated **B-cells** population from Course 3, and this run's unsupervised **UMAP B Cells**. Next, you'll add a Pipeline **AND** logic node and wire both of them into it — its output is only the events BOTH methods agree are B-cells, which is exactly how you sanity-check an unsupervised result against ground truth you already trust.

steps.section: Spotlight the Leukocytes / UMAP Reduction / UMAP B Cells trio
steps.text:
Three logic gates, one family 🔢

The Pipeline has three logic nodes, all combining populations you've already gated: **AND** keeps only events present in every connected parent — what you're about to use, for agreement between two methods. **OR** keeps events present in any connected parent — useful for merging two alternate definitions of the same population into one. **NOT** keeps events from the first parent while excluding a second — useful for an exclusion population, like 'everything that isn't a T-cell.' This course only needs AND, but OR and NOT are there whenever a real analysis calls for them.
Click '+ AND' (highlighted) to create a new logic node.

Drag it out of the way 🖐️

The new AND node has no parents yet, so it lands wherever the auto-layout puts it — possibly right on top of another node. Drag it out to the far right of the canvas, clear of everything else, before wiring it up.
Drag a connection from **UMAP B Cells** into the new AND node, then drag another from your manual **B-cells** node into it too.
Crunching the real overlap between both methods...

Read the AND node's two overlap rows 🔢

You predicted: **{answer:c4_umap_in_gate}**.

**% of UMAP B Cells** sits close to 100% — nearly every UMAP-clustered B-cell really is inside your hand-gated boundary too. No correction needed there: both sides only ever looked at the same 25% subsample, so the ratio between them is already honest as-is.

**% of B-cells** is the one to watch, and it's the one marked as an estimate. The AND's overlap only exists inside that same 25% subsample, so dividing it straight into your **full** B-cells count would make two methods that mostly agree look like they barely overlap. The app scales that overlap back up to the full population first, so the marked number is close to your true agreement rate — an honest estimate, not a silent undercount. Hover it for the exact scale factor.

Same trick everywhere a UMAP population feeds a calculation: the number marked as an estimate is the one worth trusting over its plain, unscaled neighbor.

Audit findings 📋

Three ways gates and clusters can disagree:
◯ **isn't in any population**: a cluster no gate holds.
⊕ **holds N different clusters**: one gate catches two groups.
✂ **cuts cluster N in two**: a gate edge runs through a cluster.
A what-if, not your data: **suppose** the lens said a gate **holds 2 different clusters**. Would that prove the gate is wrong?

How good is it? 🎯

The bar above scores the last step against the cluster:

• **Precision**: the share of the caught cells that are in the cluster.
• **F1**: both in one number. 1.0 would be a perfect match.
Say recall is **99%** but precision is **77%**. What does that tell you about the proposed gates?

courses.title: Second Opinions: FlowSOM & PhenoGraph
courses.description: Run two more clustering methods on the cells UMAP clustered: read FlowSOM's tree and PhenoGraph's cluster graph, see how each chooses its grain, then ask the Sample Lens which findings the methods agree on.

steps.text:
Welcome to Course 6! 🩺

UMAP + HDBSCAN gave you one opinion on Sample C. Today you ask two more methods that work differently:
• **FlowSOM**, the method most used in cytometry, where you choose how many populations (**k**).
• **PhenoGraph**, which links each cell to its most similar cells and lets the links decide; you choose how fine (**resolution**).

Then the Sample Lens shows which findings they agree on.

Make a prediction 🔮

In Course 5, UMAP + HDBSCAN had nothing left to say about your gates. Asked the same question, what will the two new methods do?

Each report something different

steps.text: Checking for your gates and Course 4's clustering run...

Missing something 🔍

This course needs the **Leukocytes**, **T-cells** and **B-cells** gates from Course 3, and Course 4's **UMAP + HDBSCAN** run on **Sample C**. Finish those courses first, then relaunch this one.

Set **Population (Gate)** to 'Leukocytes'.

FlowSOM 🌳

HDBSCAN found clusters by **density** and set the scattered cells aside as noise (cluster -1).

**FlowSOM** works differently: it sorts the cells into about 100 small groups called **nodes**, links similar nodes into a tree, and groups the tree into **metaclusters**, its populations.

Make a prediction 🔮

HDBSCAN set some cells aside as noise. What will FlowSOM do with those same cells?

Collect them in one noise metacluster
Put them in a metacluster, like every other cell

steps.text:
FlowSOM's settings ⚙️

**Grid size** 10 means 10 × 10 = 100 nodes.
**Metaclusters (k)** is how many populations to make: roughly how many cell types you expect. Leave it at 10 for now; you'll change it after the run.
**Training passes** can stay.

**Events used** jumped to 100%: FlowSOM is fast enough for every cell.
Name the run, e.g. **Sample C FlowSOM**, and click **🧬 Run Analysis**. It takes a few seconds.

The FlowSOM tree 🌳

Each circle is a **node**: a small group of very similar cells. Bigger circle, more cells.
Lines join each node to the nodes most like it, so a branch is a family of related cells.
Colours are the metaclusters.

Like UMAP's axes, positions and line lengths mean nothing. Only the connections do.
Scientists read this tree one marker at a time. Open **Colour by** and pick **CD3**, the T-cell marker.

The bright nodes are your T cells 💡

They sit together on their own branches: the tree keeps related cells together. Colour runs from the dimmest node to the brightest, so even small differences show.

Hover a bright node: the bottom right shows its cells and its metacluster's phenotype.
Now colour by **B220**, the B-cell marker.
B220 lights up a big part of the tree: your B cells 🅱️

Naming metaclusters 🧬

Each legend line gives a metacluster's share of cells and its **phenotype**. Per marker, the dimmest metacluster is **−**, the brightest **+**, and **lo** is in between. The heatmap shows the same for every marker at once.

**B220+ CD3−** is B cells, **CD3+ CD4+** CD4 T cells, **CD3+ CD8+** CD8 T cells.

steps.text:
You predicted: **{answer:cm_flowsom_noise}**.

FlowSOM put **every** cell in a metacluster: the legend's shares add up to 100%. HDBSCAN's noise cells landed with whichever population they're nearest. Remember that: it shapes what the lens says about FlowSOM later.

PhenoGraph 🕸️

PhenoGraph links each cell to its **30 most similar cells**, then links two cells more strongly the more of those neighbours they share. Groups of cells linked more to each other than to the rest become **clusters**.

You don't choose how many: **resolution** sets how finely the links are divided. Only clusters smaller than 10 cells are set aside, so there's almost no noise.

More than 10

Set **Algorithm** to **PhenoGraph**. PI and CD45 should still be unchecked in the channel list.

steps.text:
PhenoGraph's settings ⚙️

**Neighbours (k)** 30 is PhenoGraph's default: how many similar cells each cell is linked to.
**Resolution** 1.0: higher gives more, smaller clusters. You can change it after the run.
**Minimum cluster size** 10: smaller clusters become outliers.

Leave them all. Every cell is used, as with FlowSOM.
Name the run, e.g. **Sample C PhenoGraph**, and click **🧬 Run Analysis**. Linking 200,000 cells takes about 15 seconds.

The cluster graph 🕸️

You predicted: **{answer:cm_pg_count}**.

The cluster graph 🕸️

You predicted: **{answer:cm_pg_count}**.

PhenoGraph found **{…} clusters**. Nobody gave it a number: at resolution 1.0, that's how many groups the links between cells form.

Each circle is a **cluster** (bigger, more cells). A line joins two clusters whose cells are each other's neighbours; the thicker, the more linked. Positions only keep linked clusters close.

steps.text: Open **Colour by** above the graph and pick **B220**.
B220 lights up your B cells 🅱️

Unlike FlowSOM, you didn't ask for that number. … Most are joined by lines: one big population, cut along a gradient of marker levels. … Few lines join them, so some may be separate B-cell groups. … clusters**: your B cells, the biggest population here 🅱️

Like FlowSOM at k = 10, PhenoGraph at resolution 1.0 splits a big population finely. Unlike FlowSOM, you didn't ask for that number.

steps.text: Standing apart 🏝️
The clusters standing apart are **B220+** and **CD3+**: a B-cell marker and a T-cell marker on the same cells. What are they?
steps.explanation: Doublets are a good suspect, and a singlet gate (FSC-H against FSC-A) would test it on data that has those channels. Until something tests it, a group that stands apart is a lead, not an answer.

choices.text: A new kind of cell
choices.feedback: Possible, but nothing here shows it. A rare, odd phenotype needs checking before it's named.

choices.text: Doublets: a B cell and a T cell stuck together
choices.feedback: A real possibility: two cells passing the laser together look like this. But these files have no FSC-H or FSC-W, so you can't gate single cells to check. Don't assume it.

steps.explanation: Resolution is PhenoGraph's k: it sets the grain, not the data. The links between cells stay the same.

choices.text: Rerun the neighbours from scratch
choices.feedback: The links stay as they are. Only how finely they're divided changes, which is why it takes seconds.

choices.text: Merge clusters into fewer, bigger ones
Split clusters into more, smaller ones

steps.text: Set **Resolution** above the graph to **0.5**. It re-clusters in a few seconds.
Fewer clusters 🔁

From **{…}** clusters to **{…}** 🔁

Clusters that were split along a gradient merged; the links between cells didn't change, only how finely they're divided. … ** 🔁

A group that keeps apart at both resolutions is a steady feature of the data. … . Merged into one cluster, its links to the rest are too weak to draw. … Still standing apart:

steps.text:
Which resolution is right? ⚖️

Neither: like FlowSOM's k and HDBSCAN's minimum cluster size, it picks the grain. Look for what holds across settings: a group that keeps standing apart, a population that stays one cluster.

Keep 0.5 for now. Next, the lens holds your gates up against both new runs.
Click the **Sample Lens** tab at the top.
Choose **Sample C** in the **Sample** dropdown.
steps.failure_hint: Open the **Sample** dropdown at the top left and pick **Sample C**.

steps.text: FlowSOM first. Pick your **FlowSOM** run in **Clustering run**.
steps.failure_hint: Open **Clustering run** and pick the run with 'FlowSOM' in its name.

steps.text:
Same lens, another method 🔍

Findings now name **metaclusters** and their phenotype, and the map is the FlowSOM tree, with a finding's nodes ringed.

FlowSOM always makes k groups, so the lens only calls it a merge when the phenotypes clearly differ, and groups findings that share a phenotype.
You left this run at k = 5. Set **Metaclusters (k)** to **8** and watch the findings.

Why these findings? 🤔

Your gates didn't change. Most of these come from how FlowSOM works:
• **No noise.** HDBSCAN leaves in-between cells out; FlowSOM puts every cell in a metacluster. A gate that skips a population's sparse edge then looks like a cut, keeping 75–90%.
• **The proposed gates** (the *Cluster* ones from Course 5) were fitted to UMAP's cluster, so FlowSOM's borders won't match them.
• **Few, broad groups.** At low k a big metacluster's edge spills into a small gate such as DN.

The grey line 🤝

Under each finding, the lens says whether your **other runs** of these cells report the same thing: *Also found by …* or *Only this run finds it*.

Cluster numbers mean nothing across runs, so it matches what findings say: the same kind of finding on the same gate, or, for missed cells, mostly the same cells.
Now pick your **PhenoGraph** run in **Clustering run**.

steps.text:
The cuts ✂️

A cut's detail says how much of the cluster the gate keeps. **80–90%** is a gate edge in a cluster's sparse tail: PhenoGraph, like FlowSOM, puts nearly every cell in a cluster, where HDBSCAN would call the tail noise.

Read those as *this edge sits in a gradient*, not *this gate is wrong*. Click one to see its cells ringed on the map.
FlowSOM and PhenoGraph both say **DN holds two clusters**, and the bigger one is **CD3−**. DN sits inside T-cells. What's the most likely story?
steps.explanation: Most of DN's cells belong to the CD3− cluster and are dimmer for CD3 than other T cells: that population's dim edge crosses the T-cells gate and lands in DN. Some may be real, but DN's number mostly reflects where the T-cells edge sits.

choices.text: DN is a new kind of CD3− T cell
choices.feedback: T cells carry CD3. A CD3− cluster inside a T-cell gate points at the gate first.

choices.text: The T-cells gate's lower CD3 edge reaches into the CD3− cells next door
Both methods are wrong
choices.feedback: Two methods that work differently agree. That's when a finding deserves a look.

steps.text: Only PhenoGraph says **DP holds two clusters**: the second is the **B220+ CD4+ CD3+ CD8+** group that stood apart in the graph. What do you do with it?
steps.explanation: A finding one method reports is a lead, not a verdict. Here the check would be a singlet gate on data that has FSC-H, or a closer look at those cells. Until then, DP's number carries a caveat.

choices.text: Gate it out of DP: they're doublets
choices.feedback: Maybe they are, but nothing here proves it, and these files can't be checked for singlets.

choices.text: Ignore it: only one method reports it
choices.feedback: One method is a reason for caution, not for ignoring it. Small, distinct groups are what PhenoGraph finds best.

choices.text: Note it, and check it another way before changing a gate

steps.text: Back to the finer grain: set the lens's **Resolution** to **1.0** and watch the findings.
Same gates, finer grain 🔬

Your gates didn't move. A finding that comes and goes with the resolution is about the method's grain; one that holds at both, and that another method shares, is about your gates. … **{…} new** finding{…} … Same gates, finer grain 🔬

At resolution 1.0: {…}. … Same gates, finer grain 🔬

At resolution 1.0: …

steps.text:
Which findings to trust ⚖️

• **Shared** by methods that work differently, and holding across settings: about your gates. Look at it (DN).
• **One method, one setting:** about the method. Set it aside.
• **One method, but steady and distinct:** a lead. Note it and check it another way (DP).

No method is the truth, the lens included. The gates are your call.

Your prediction 🔮

At the start you predicted: **{answer:cm_methods_agree}**.

They agreed on some findings and not others. Where HDBSCAN set in-between cells aside, FlowSOM and PhenoGraph put them in clusters, so they saw edges UMAP didn't, and the agreement line sorted the shared findings from the method's own.

courses.title: Derived Parameters, Statistics & Comparisons
courses.description: Build a per-cell B220 ÷ CD45 derived parameter, then use your Course 4 populations — the hand-gated B-cells and the UMAP-exported UMAP B Cells — to test whether they measure the same, with the Statistics table and charts and the Comparisons charts.

steps.text:
Welcome to Course 7! 📊

Course 4 left you with two independent ways of finding B-cells — your own hand-gated **B-cells**, and the unsupervised **UMAP B Cells** — plus an AND node showing they're nearly the same cells.

This course asks the next question: are they also **measured** the same? You'll answer it with a new kind of parameter, real statistics and side-by-side charts.

What you'll walk away with 🎯

By the end of this course, you'll be able to:
• Build a derived parameter — a per-cell formula like B220 ÷ CD45 — and plot, gate and measure it like any channel
• Pick the statistic that makes a fair comparison between samples, and read it from a lean table
• Choose a Statistics chart that keeps long population names readable
• Choose the right Comparisons chart (Violin, Channel Heatmap, Histogram Overlay, Pseudocolor Overlay) for a question about two populations
• Export your tables and plots

Make a prediction 🔮

UMAP B Cells and your hand-gated B-cells are nearly the same cells. Measured on B220, how will UMAP's B cells compare with yours? There's no wrong answer — we'll check at the end.

choices.text: About the same peak and spread
Brighter — UMAP keeps the clearest B cells
Dimmer — UMAP lets in borderline cells
Much broader — clustering is messier

steps.text: Checking for your Course 4 analysis...

Missing your Course 4 export 🔍

Course 7 needs the **UMAP B Cells** population and the **AND** node cross-checking it against **B-cells** — both built in Course 4. Head back and finish that course first, then relaunch Course 7.

New tool: derived parameters ƒ

Every cell is just a row of numbers — FSC, SSC, one per detector. A **derived parameter** is a new number you calculate for every cell from the ones it already has, e.g. **GFP ÷ RFP**.

That exact ratio is a classic in reporter experiments: RFP on a constant promoter says how much plasmid a cell got, GFP says how active your promoter is — dividing one by the other cancels out the lucky-transfection noise. Once built, a derived parameter works like a real channel: plot it, gate on it, compute statistics on it.

Our version: B220 ÷ CD45 🧬

Our panel has no GFP, but it has the same idea built in. **CD45** is on every leukocyte — our "RFP", a reference for how much a cell is staining overall. **B220** is itself a B-cell form of CD45 (CD45R).

So **B220 ÷ CD45** asks, per cell: *how much of this cell's CD45 signal is the B-cell kind?* Let's build it on Sample C's Leukocytes.
In the Data hierarchy, right-click **Sample C**, then click **Leukocytes** in the population menu — the same move you made in Course 3.
Checking opened population...
Oops! Right-click **Sample C** and choose **Leukocytes** from its menu.
Open the **Gating** tab (its ribbon has the tool we need).
Click **ƒ Derived** (highlighted) on the Gating ribbon.

Build the ratio ➗

In the Derived Parameters window:
• **Start from:** Ratio A ÷ B
• **A:** B220 (FITC-A) — the marker, on top
• **B:** CD45 (APC-A) — the reference, underneath

The formula fills itself in as **[FITC-A] / [APC-A]** and the name as **B220/CD45** — keep both, then click **Save**.
steps.failure_hint: Pick Ratio A ÷ B, set A to B220 (FITC-A) and B to CD45 (APC-A), then click Save.

steps.text:
What the preview shows 🔍

Your formula has already been run on every cell in Sample C — the chart is the result, before you save anything.

• **Left to right** — each cell's B220 ÷ CD45. Left = little B220 for its CD45, right = lots. The marks **0.01**, **0.1**, **1** are each 10× the one before.
• **Bar height** — how many cells have that value.
• **Grey** — the whole sample. It has **two humps**: two kinds of cell with very different amounts of B220.
• **Blue** — only the population picked in the dropdown, so you can see which hump is which.

Before you switch 🤔

If you picked **T-cells** in the preview's dropdown, which hump would the blue bars land on?
steps.explanation: T cells carry plenty of CD45 but almost no B220, so their ratio is tiny. Switch the dropdown next and check.

choices.text: The right hump, near 0.6
choices.feedback: That's where cells with lots of B220 sit — and B220 is a B-cell marker.

choices.text: The left hump, near 0.01
Both humps equally
choices.feedback: Each cell has one ratio, and T cells are alike here: lots of CD45, very little B220.

steps.text:
Check it 🔬

Switch the preview's population dropdown:
• **T-cells** — blue sits on the **left** hump, near **0.01**.
• **B-cells** — blue jumps to the **right** hump, near **0.6**.

The line under the chart puts numbers on it:
• **median** — the ratio of a typical cell in that population.
• **% invalid** — cells where the ratio can't be computed (CD45 at or below zero). ~0% here, so CD45 is a safe thing to divide by.

That's the point of the preview: check the parameter does what you meant **before** you save it and gate on it.
Close the Derived Parameters window (**Close**, highlighted).
Switch the graph's plot type to **Histogram**.

Now set the **X:** axis to **ƒ B220/CD45** — derived parameters are listed after the real channels.

(The **＋ New derived parameter…** entry at the very bottom is a shortcut: anything you build from there lands straight on that axis.)

The preview, full size 📊

This is the same picture as the preview, now on a real graph you can gate on:
• **X axis** — each cell's own **B220 ÷ CD45** value. It's a **log** scale (the Ratio template's default): **10⁻²** = 0.01, **10⁻¹** = 0.1, **10⁰** = 1, each step 10× the one before, so small and large ratios both get room.
• **Y axis** — **Count**: how many cells fall in each thin slice of X.

So every **peak** is a group of cells sharing a similar ratio — one peak per kind of cell.

Two populations, one axis 🔬

• **Left peak, near 0.01** — leukocytes with almost no B220: **T cells** and other non-B leukocytes. Broad, because their B220 is just background noise — dividing noise by CD45 smears it across decades.
• **Right peak, near 0.6** — **B cells**. Tall (most of Sample C's leukocytes are B cells) and **narrow**: bright B220 over bright CD45 varies only a little from cell to cell.

The peaks sit ~60× apart, so a **Range gate** on the right peak, drawn inside Leukocytes, picks out B cells — ~97% pure in this data. Keep it inside Leukocytes: a cell with almost no CD45 gets a big ratio from almost no B220.

Ratio rules of thumb ⚠️

• **Compensate first** — a ratio of uncompensated channels includes spillover.
• **Relative units** — FITC and APC differ in brightness, so 0.6 doesn't mean 60% of CD45 is B220. Compare ratios between cells and samples measured on the same panel, not as absolute values.

Your turn 🧠

On another panel, a ratio shows **40% invalid** events in one population and ~0% everywhere else. What's the most likely cause?
steps.explanation: Dividing by a value at or below zero has no meaningful answer, so those cells are marked invalid. A dim denominator makes the ratio mostly noise — pick a reference that's bright on every cell you care about, like CD45 here.

choices.text: The numerator is very bright there
choices.feedback: A bright numerator just gives a big ratio. Invalid means the value can't be computed — dividing by ≤ 0.

choices.text: The axis is on a log scale
choices.feedback: The scale only changes how values are drawn. % invalid counts cells whose ratio can't be computed at all.

choices.text: The denominator is dim — near or below zero — in that population
The population has too many events
choices.feedback: % invalid is a share, so event count doesn't drive it. Look at what's being divided by.

steps.text: Now put numbers on it — click the **Statistics** tab at the top.

First, brightness 💡

B220 spans four decades on a log axis, and a few cells are far brighter than the rest. Which number best describes how bright a **typical** B cell is?
steps.explanation: Half the cells are dimmer than the median and half brighter, so a few extreme cells barely move it — that's why MFI is the standard brightness statistic in flow.

choices.text: The median (MFI)
The arithmetic mean
choices.feedback: A handful of very bright cells drag the mean upward on log-scaled data, so it overstates a typical cell.

choices.text: The maximum
choices.feedback: The maximum is one extreme cell — often an outlier or a doublet — not a typical one.

choices.text: % Total
choices.feedback: % Total measures how many cells there are, not how bright they are.

steps.text:
Trim the population list 🎯

Click **Edit Population Selection** (highlighted) to open the picker — a grid of populations × samples you can drag to move and resize from its corner for more room. Every population starts checked by default — click **None** first, then check 4 cells total:

• **B-cells** — check it in the **Sample A**, **B** and **C** columns. Not the row label: in Course 3 the gate propagated to *every* sample, controls included, so the row would tick all 10.
• **UMAP B Cells** — only exists on **Sample C**, where you built it; check just that one cell.

Once your 4 cells are checked, close the popup (✕, Esc, or click outside it) to continue.

A fair comparison ⚖️

Leukocytes are 89% of Sample A's events, 77% of B's and only 65% of C's — the rest is debris and dead cells. To compare **how much of each sample's immune cells are B cells**, which statistic?
steps.explanation: % Parent divides by the gate above — here Leukocytes — so debris drops out. In this data % Total says C has 1.35× B's share of B cells; % of Leukocytes says 1.6×.

choices.text: % Total — the share of every event
choices.feedback: % Total divides by debris and dead cells too, so a messier sample looks like it has fewer B cells.

choices.text: Count
choices.feedback: Count depends on how many events were recorded, which differs between tubes.

choices.text: % Parent — the share of Leukocytes
CV
choices.feedback: CV is how spread out a peak is, not how many cells there are.

steps.text:
Trim the stat list too ✂️

**Count**, **Percent Parent** and **MFI** are checked by default — keep **Percent Parent** (that's % Parent), uncheck the other two, and check **Cv** (how spread out a peak is: high CV = broad, messy population).

That **★** next to CV means it needs a fluorescence channel picked below — % Parent doesn't, since it counts cells rather than measuring a marker.

Give CV its ★ channel ƒ

In the **Channel** dropdown (highlighted), pick **ƒ B220/CD45** — your derived parameter works here like any detector.
Click '📊 Compute Statistics' (highlighted) to generate the table. Cyto carries on once it's ready.

Read the table 🔍

Look along the **B-cells** row's **Percent Parent** columns. Which sample has almost no B cells?
steps.explanation: Sample A is the thymus, where T cells mature — B cells are 0.4% of its Leukocytes, against 43% in bone marrow (B) and 68% in spleen (C): Course 3's mystery, in numbers.

choices.text: Sample A
Sample B
choices.feedback: B's B-cells are a solid ~43% of its Leukocytes. Look for a value well under 1%.

choices.text: Sample C
choices.feedback: C has the most — ~68% of its Leukocytes. Look for a value well under 1%.

steps.text: Click '📈 Chart' (highlighted) to switch from table to chart view.

Read the chart 📈

With **Cv** picked in the dropdown beside the chart type, the bars show each population's CV on **B220 ÷ CD45**. Sample B's B-cells have the lowest. What does that tell you?
steps.explanation: CV is the standard deviation divided by the mean: spread, scaled to the average. B's B cells sit tightest (~35%); Sample A's ~75% comes from only ~1,000 cells — too few for a clean peak.

choices.text: It has the most B cells
choices.feedback: That's % Parent's job. CV ignores how many cells there are — only how spread out their values are.

choices.text: Its B cells' ratios are the most alike — the tightest peak
Its B cells have the highest ratio
choices.feedback: CV is spread relative to the average, so a population can be bright and broad, or dim and tight.

steps.text: Bars get crowded as populations pile up. Switch the chart-type dropdown (highlighted) to **Heatmap** — a grid that stays readable.

One-glance comparison 🗺️

Rows are populations, columns are samples; the dropdown next to the chart type picks which statistic fills the cells.

Switch it to **Percent Parent** and look at Sample C: your B-cells are **68%** of Leukocytes, UMAP B Cells **64%** of the Leukocytes UMAP ran on. Close, with UMAP a little stricter — one clue for your prediction.
Numbers done; now shapes. Click the **Comparisons** tab at the top.

Comparing distributions 🎨

Statistics gave single numbers; this tab plots the whole *distribution* of each population. Four chart types, each answering a different question about your two B-cell methods.

Pick your population here too 🎯

This tab has its own population picker, separate from the one on the Statistics tab. Click **Edit Population Selection** (highlighted) and check **B-cells** in the **Sample A**, **B** and **C** columns (the row label would tick the controls too).

Violin (the first chart type below) only allows one population per sample, so this is the one to use for it. A later step brings **UMAP B Cells** into the mix once you reach a chart type that can show more than one population per sample. Close the popup (✕, Esc, or click outside it) once you're done.
Select '🎻 Violin Plot'.

Before you generate: what these settings do 🎛️

• **Orientation** — vertical or horizontal violins.
• **Axis Range** — clips the axis to a percentile so a few bright outliers don't squash the rest of the distribution into a sliver near zero. Leave at 100 for the full range.
• **Show box plot overlay** — draws median/IQR whiskers inside each violin.
• **Show individual data points** — overlays up to 500 raw events per sample as dots.
Click '🔬 Generate Plot' (highlighted) to render it with the settings from the last step. Cyto carries on once it's ready.
Wide violin = many cells at that intensity. Three organs, one population — the same Thymus/Bone Marrow/Spleen B-cell story as the table, now as shape instead of a percentage.
Select '🗺️ Channel Heatmap'.

Bring in UMAP B Cells 🎯

Heatmap (and every chart type from here on) can show more than one population per sample, unlike Violin. Open **Edit Population Selection** (highlighted) again and also check **UMAP B Cells** for Sample C — leave your existing B-cells checks alone, just add this one. Now you have both methods side by side: the real comparison this whole course has been building to.

Close the popup once you're done.

About that Channels list 📡

Violin only ever used one channel, so switching here reset the checklist back to **everything checked** — channel checks only carry over between chart types that share the same single-vs-multi channel mode, never across a mode change. Leave everything checked, or trim to just the channels you care about (e.g. B220) for a cleaner grid.
Click '🔬 Generate Plot' (highlighted) to render it. Cyto carries on once it's ready.

Every marker at once 🗺️

Both Sample C B-cell rows should light up the same way, marker by marker — the same **profile**, not just the same B220.

(The **Radar Chart** in the same dropdown draws this as one shape per population — handy for big panels with many markers. We'll skip it here.)
Select '📊 Histogram Overlay'.

What these settings do 🎛️

• **Layout** — Ridge (the default, also called 'waterfall') stacks each population in its own row; Overlay draws them all on one shared axis instead.
• **Smooth curve (KDE)** — a smooth density estimate instead of raw histogram bars.
• **Normalise to peak** — scales each curve so its own peak hits 1.0, so a small population stays visible next to a big one. Turn off to compare absolute event counts.
• **X-axis scale** — Linear, Log₁₀, or Biexponential.

The Channels list reset again — Channel Heatmap was multi-channel, Histogram is single-channel.

Set it up to test your prediction 🔀

• **Channels:** check only **ƒ B220/CD45** — your ratio.
• **Layout:** pick **'Overlay (all on one axis)'**, so the curves sit on top of each other.
Click '🔬 Generate Plot' (highlighted) to render it. Cyto carries on once it's ready.

Your prediction, tested 🔮

You predicted: **{answer:c6_same_measure}**.

Find Sample C's two curves — B-cells and UMAP B Cells. They sit almost on top of each other: median ratio **0.64** vs **0.65**, and a near-identical spread (CV **46%** vs **44%**). B220 alone says the same: medians within 1%. Same cells, measured the same — UMAP's just a touch tighter.

(Sample A's lumpy curve comes from only ~1,000 thymus B cells — too few for a clean peak.)
Last chart type: select '🌈 Pseudocolor Overlay'.
Click '🔬 Generate Plot' (highlighted) to render it. Cyto carries on once it's ready.

A different kind of comparison 🌈

This one skips channel expression entirely — no shared Channels list at all this time, because it isn't comparing a marker's intensity. It overlays population *shapes* on one sample, side by side, using its own X/Y Axis Channel pickers in **Plot Options** instead. Good for sanity-checking that your manual and UMAP-derived B-cells actually occupy the same region on a real 2D plot, not just matching numbers.

Take it with you 📤

Both tabs export. Do these two, in either order — Cyto carries on once both files are saved.

Also worth knowing: **📋 Copy All** on Statistics puts the table on your clipboard, and its Chart view has its own **📸 Export**.

sub_tasks.instruction: Here on Comparisons: '📸 Export' saves this plot (PNG, PDF or SVG).
On Statistics: '📤 Export CSV' saves the table for a spreadsheet.

steps.text: Last step: save your progress. Click the **⚠️ Save Workspace** button (highlighted) at the top right.

steps.text:
Course 7 is complete — you're officially an **Insight Reporter**! 🏆

**The verdict.** You predicted: *{answer:c6_same_measure}*. The evidence:
• **Same cells** — 99.95% of UMAP B Cells sit inside your gate, and UMAP found ~93% of yours.
• **Same measurement** — ratio peaks at 0.64 vs 0.65, with matching spread and marker profiles.

Two independent methods, one answer — that's the kind of cross-check worth putting in a report.

steps.text: 🧬 Welcome to **Flow Cytometry**! Every module gets a workspace built just for what it does.

One thing before you import anything: Karcytics never touches your raw files. On import, it hashes the file (SHA-256) and copies it into this project's `` `assets/` `` folder — your original stays exactly where it was.
Can we download a demo FCS file into your Downloads folder to use for this tutorial? If you decline, you will need to provide your own valid FCS file.
No problem! Please click **➕ Add Samples** (highlighted) and import any valid FCS file from your machine to continue.

I've dropped a demo file (`` `demo_tutorial.fcs` ``) in your Downloads folder.

Click **➕ Add Samples** (highlighted) and pick it. When it asks whether to copy the file into your workspace, say yes.
Loaded! A **Workflow** is a snapshot of everything right now — settings, gates, parameters — so you can pick this exact session back up later.
Let's lock this in. Click **Save Workspace** (highlighted).
Saved! 🎉 Every module also has its own preferences. Open them from {…}
These are Flow Cytometry's own preferences. Click **Workspace** in the list on the left.
steps.failure_hint: Closed Preferences? Reopen it from {…}, then click **Workspace**.

steps.text:
Tick **Autosave workflows every 15 minutes** and Karcytics will quietly re-save your workflow for you. It only kicks in once a workflow has been saved manually — which you just did. Leave it off and you'll get a gentle reminder every 15 minutes instead.

Close **Preferences** whenever you're ready to continue.
All set! Close this window (File → Close, or the OS close button) to head back to Karcytics — Cyto's waiting for you there.
